\chapter{Sorry}
\label{ch:ar-sorry}
\hlchaptermodality{7}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can apologise in Arabic with āsif or āsifa, choosing the form that matches who is speaking.}

Say the apology twice -- āsif for a man, āsifa for a woman -- then the ungendered maʿdhira.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ar{آسف} / \ar{آسفة}]{\ar{آسف} / \ar{آسفة} (āsif / āsifa) — sorry}

\label{lesson:AR-C07-asif}



\begin{quote}
You already know \textbf{\ar{من} \ar{فضلك}}, \textquotedblleft{}please.\textquotedblright{} Arabic's word for \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{} teaches a new lesson entirely: it isn't a fixed word at all — \textbf{it changes with the speaker.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{آسف}} (\emph{āsif}, said by a man) and \textbf{\ar{آسفة}} (\emph{āsifa}, said by a woman) both mean \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{sorry}.\textquotedblright{} They come from the verb \textbf{\ar{أَسِفَ}} (\emph{asifa}), \textquotedblleft{}to grieve, to be filled with regret\textquotedblright{} — so saying \emph{āsif} is describing yourself as \emph{grieved / regretful}, the way you'd say \textquotedblleft{}I am tired\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}I am happy.\textquotedblright{}

That's the key: \textbf{\ar{آسف} is an adjective}, and Arabic adjectives \textbf{agree with the gender of the person they describe}. A man says \textbf{\ar{آسف}}; a woman says \textbf{\ar{آسفة}} — the extra \textbf{\ar{ة}} (\emph{tāʾ marbūṭa}) is the everyday feminine ending you'll meet across Arabic adjectives. English \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{} never changes no matter who says it; Arabic \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{} always tells you the speaker's gender in the same breath.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
For a quick, \textbf{ungendered} \textquotedblleft{}excuse me / pardon\textquotedblright{} — squeezing past someone, interrupting, a light apology — Arabic reaches for \textbf{\ar{معذرة}} (\emph{maʿdhira}), from the root \textbf{\ar{ع}-\ar{ذ}-\ar{ر}} (\textquotedblleft{}to excuse\textquotedblright{}), the same root as \textbf{\ar{عذر}} (\emph{ʿudhr}, \textquotedblleft{}an excuse\textquotedblright{}) and the verb \textbf{\ar{يعتذر}} (\emph{yaʿtadhiru}, \textquotedblleft{}to apologize\textquotedblright{}). Unlike \emph{āsif/āsifa}, \textbf{\ar{معذرة} doesn't change with gender} — it's a noun, not an adjective, so anyone says the same word.

Use \textbf{\ar{آسف}/\ar{آسفة}} when you mean a real, felt \textquotedblleft{}I'm sorry\textquotedblright{} (and remember to match your own gender); reach for \textbf{\ar{معذرة}} for the light, everyday \textquotedblleft{}pardon me.\textquotedblright{}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a man says — \textquotedblleft{}āsif\textquotedblright{}
  \item a woman says — \textquotedblleft{}āsifa\textquotedblright{}
  \item the ungendered one — \textquotedblleft{}maʿdhira\textquotedblright{} = excuse me / pardon
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What's unusual about \textbf{\ar{آسف} / \ar{آسفة}} compared to English \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{It's a gendered adjective} — \emph{āsif} for a man, \emph{āsifa} for a woman — where English never changes.) What root gives \emph{āsif}, and what does it mean? (\textbf{\ar{أسف} asafa}, \textquotedblleft{}to grieve, regret.\textquotedblright{}) What's the ungendered word for a quick \textquotedblleft{}excuse me,\textquotedblright{} and what root is it from? (\textbf{\ar{معذرة} maʿdhira}, from \textbf{\ar{ع}-\ar{ذ}-\ar{ر}} \textquotedblleft{}to excuse.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
